sections.title: Introduction

paragraphs.en: The genus Enterovirus within the family Picornaviridae comprises over 250 clinically significant serotypes that circulate worldwide [1–3]. Enterovirus infections manifest with a diverse spectrum of clinical presentations, including upper and lower respiratory tract illnesses, gastroenteritis, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, conjunctivitis, myocarditis, severe neonatal sepsis-like disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis (AFP), and AFM [3–6]. Important human pathogens within this genus include coxsackieviruses, enterovirus A71 (EVA71), enterovirus D68 (EVD68), echoviruses, and poliovirus (PV) [7–9]. Although these viruses share characteristics such as a small genome, rapid evolution, and broad pathogenic spectrum, targeted antiviral drugs remain absent. The functional pleiotropy of nonstructural protein 2B has emerged as a major obstacle to rational drug design. Understanding how a single ~100-amino-acid protein can engage in such disparate pathways is the central question addressed in this review.

Enteroviruses possess a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome of approximately 7.5 kb in length [10–12]. A single open reading frame encodes a polyprotein that is proteolytically processed into three precursor regions: P1 (structural proteins VP1–VP4) and non-structural regions P2 and P3 [13]. The 2B protein, together with 2A (protease) [14,15] and 2C (helicase/ATPase) [16–18], constitutes the P2 region of the viral genome. Whereas 2A and 3C perform well-defined enzymatic functions, namely the proteolytic cleavage of viral and host targets [19,20], 2B is remarkable for its broad functional repertoire. Understanding how a single ~100-amino-acid protein can engage in such disparate pathways is the central question addressed in this review.

The 2B protein is a non-structural protein of approximately 100 amino acids, encoded by the enterovirus genome [21,22]. Since its discovery in the 1980s, it has been defined as a “viroporin,” a protein that disrupts ion homeostasis by forming transmembrane hydrophilic pores [23–25]. Across viral families, viroporins share conserved strategies of membrane perturbation, including pore formation, lipid bilayer disordering, and membrane curvature sensing, underscoring the evolutionary convergence of these mechanisms [26,27]. Well-characterized examples include HCV p7, influenza A M2, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) Vpu, each of which exploits distinct membrane-targeting mechanisms while sharing a common capacity to dysregulate host ion homeostasis [28–31]. The enterovirus 2B protein extends this paradigm with a uniquely dynamic topology that may enable membrane stress sensing. This framework, which has dominated research for three decades, successfully explains the effects of 2B on calcium signaling and membrane permeability during early viral replication. However, intensive research over the past decade has revealed a functional breadth that far exceeds the scope of traditional pore models.

sections.title: Limitations of the viroporin model and the membrane stress sensor hypothesis

paragraphs.en: First, the pore model cannot explain the breadth of protein–protein interactions (PPI) in cell membranes. 2B has been shown to directly interacts with multiple host proteins, including Bax [32], NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) [33], Karyopherin subunit alpha 1 (KPNA1) [34], Interleukin enhancer-binding factor 2 (ILF2) [35], Cluster of Differentiation 74 (CD74) [36], Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel 3 (VDAC3) [37], and N-Acetyltransferase 8 (NAT8) [38]. These interactions span apoptosis, inflammation, nuclear transport, and immune recognition, extending far beyond the scope of ion-channel activity.

Second, the pore model cannot explain species-specific functional divergence. The stable association of EVD68 2B with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane depends on an acidic environment; when autophagic flux is blocked and vesicle acidification is insufficient, 2B cannot be stably anchored to the membrane [39], a phenomenon not observed for coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) or PV. The E40K mutation in CVB3 2B produces a quasi-infectious phenotype that can be rescued by trans-complementation [40], suggesting differences in the functional plasticity among enterovirus 2B proteins. Moreover, the subcellular localization differs: CVB3 2B is primarily localized to the Golgi apparatus, whereas PV 2B exhibits a distinct topological orientation [22,41].

Third, the pore model cannot accommodate discrepancies between functional redundancy and pore essentiality. The impact of 2B deletion on viral replication varies considerably among viruses: siRNA-mediated knockdown of EVA71 2B markedly reduces but does not abolish viral replication [42], while a CVB3 2B-derived peptide potently inhibits the virus without achieving sterilizing clearance [43].

Fourth, the pore model cannot incorporate post-transcriptional RNA-level regulation, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of Lon Peptidase 1 (LONP1) mRNA. A direct RNA-modification link between 2B and ferroptosis was established in a recent study [44].

In summary, the existing framework can no longer accommodate the functional breadth and depth of 2B. Studies have shown that the transmembrane helices of 2B can respond with conformational sensitivity to physicochemical parameters, such as membrane lipid composition and pH, with distinct conformational states corresponding to different downstream effector outputs, a characteristic that endows 2B with “sensor” functionality. Therefore, this study proposes a new theoretical framework: defining 2B as a membrane stress sensor, whose diverse functional outputs arise from its conformational responsiveness to changes in the membrane microenvironment. This framework comprises three operational criteria.

We emphasize that this framework is a testable working hypothesis and not a validated mechanism. Direct experimental evidence for conformational switching under different membrane conditions is currently lacking, and the three operational criteria defined below remain to be experimentally verified.

sections.title: Conformational responsiveness to changes in the membrane microenvironment

paragraphs.en: The transmembrane helices (H1/H2) and stem-loop hinge region of 2B adopt different conformational states in different membrane environments. These environmental parameters include lipid composition, membrane curvature, and pH values. These conformational states can be captured using structural biology approaches [e.g. such as fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)].

sections.title: Distinct conformational states correspond to different functional outputs

paragraphs.en: Specific conformational states can expose different protein interaction interfaces, thereby selectively activating pathways such as calcium signaling, apoptosis, pyroptosis, and immune evasion. Conformation-locking mutants exhibit directional changes in their functional spectra.

sections.title: Membrane microenvironment is essential for functional switching

paragraphs.en: The functional switching of 2B strictly depends on changes in the membrane environmental parameters. For example, differences in lipid composition among the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial, and autophagosomal membranes may directly determine whether 2B activates Bax or NLRP3, and disruption of the pH gradient can lead to 2B degradation or its inactivation.

Throughout this review, we distinguished three categories of evidence: (i) experimentally validated: conclusions directly supported by published experimental data, including mutagenesis, co-immunoprecipitation, FRET, and functional assays. (ii) Inferred from indirect evidence: conclusions consistent with the available data but not yet confirmed by direct experimentation. (iii) Speculative: components of the membrane stress sensor hypothesis that generate testable predictions but currently lack experimental support. All speculative statements are explicitly identified in the text.

We elaborate on this framework across six dimensions: structure–function mapping, calcium signaling, cell death regulation (encompassing apoptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy, and ferroptosis), immune evasion, evolutionary footprint, and antiviral targeting.

sections.title: Structural basis: conformational dynamics of the transmembrane helices
Conservation and diversity of the transmembrane topology

paragraphs.en: The transmembrane helices constitute the functional core of the 2B protein. Studies using CVB3 2B as a model have shown that the protein contains two hydrophobic transmembrane regions (H1 and H2) connected by a hydrophilic stem loop, forming a typical class IIA viroporin topology [23,24,41]. H1 mediates insertion into the ER membrane, whereas H2 participates in oligomerization to form tetrameric pores. A single point mutation, V56A (located in the stem loop), completely abolishes the ability to induce autophagy, indicating that this region is crucial for conformational stability [45]. Mutational analysis and mammalian two-hybrid experiments further confirmed that the stem-loop region of 2B (particularly the58 RNHDD62 motif) is essential for its multimerization and membrane permeabilization activities [46,47].

However, the topological types of these viruses differ. PV 2B and EVA71 2B adopt a type IIB topology (both N- and C-termini facing the cytosol), whereas CVB3 2B adopts a type IIA topology (both termini facing the lumen) [23,48]. This topological difference may affect accessibility to different host factors and represents a structural basis for the functional divergence. For instance, a cytosol-facing C-terminus would be more accessible to cytosolic proteins such as Bax and KPNA1, whereas a lumen-facing C-terminus may participate in calcium regulation within the ER lumen.

Evidence of domain-specific functional partitioning further supports the conformational dynamics hypothesis. The mitochondrial localization of EVA71 2B depends on its C-terminal 18 amino acids (aa 63–80), whereas the Bax-binding function resides in the N-terminal 14 amino acids (aa 22–35) [32]. The ability of different domains within the same protein to independently execute functions is a prerequisite for conformational dynamics, as different conformational states can expose different domains, thereby enabling functional switching.

Furthermore, the oligomeric state of 2B influences its function; FRET experiments have shown that CVB3 2B forms homomultimers in living cells [49], and mutational analysis has demonstrated that disruption of multimerization severely impairs viral RNA replication [46]. Beyond homomeric interactions, 2B engages in heteromeric contacts with other nonstructural proteins. Yeast two-hybrid analysis of poliovirus proteins revealed that 2B interacts with 3A and 3AB [50], physically linking the P2 and P3 replication modules within the viral replication complex. Consistent with this, enterovirus infection induces the massive recruitment of small Arf GTPases to replication organelles; notably, Arf1 is the first to be recruited and strongly colocalizes with 2B and mature virions, but not with double-stranded RNA [51]. This spatial segregation—2B associated with mature virions but not with actively replicating RNA–suggests that 2B may function beyond the initial stages of RNA replication, potentially in later steps, such as virion maturation or release.

Despite decades of investigation, the high-resolution three-dimensional structure of 2B in a native membrane environment remains elusive. Conventional structural biology methods have proven inadequate for resolving the conformation of small transmembrane helices within lipid bilayers; however, recent technical advances offer a viable pathway. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy has demonstrated exceptional power in resolving transmembrane helix conformation within lipid environments [52], while cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography have enabled near-atomic visualization of membrane protein complexes and viral transport processes that were previously intractable [53–55]. Integrating these emerging experimental approaches with comprehensive reviews of membrane protein structural biology will be essential to resolve outstanding questions regarding the 2B oligomerization state and lipid-dependent conformational switching [56].

Central to advancing this structural understanding is the “membrane stress sensor” hypothesis, which posits that 2B undergoes Ca2+- and lipid-composition-dependent conformational transitions between “open” and “closed” pore states. Real-time monitoring of 2B conformational dynamics in living cells is now feasible using FRET-based biosensors, an approach that has successfully captured dynamic rearrangements in ion channels and signaling proteins [57–59]. FRET-based single-molecule imaging has resolved sub-angstrom conformational rearrangements in voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels in living cells [60,61], providing a technical blueprint for directly measuring 2B conformational switching in response to membrane tension or lipid composition changes. Complementarily, solid-state NMR methods capable of resolving helix-tilt angles and side-chain rotamers in membrane-embedded peptides can determine whether the putative gating helix undergoes the predicted reorientation in response to Ca2+ depletion [52]. Implementing these approaches would directly test the membrane stress sensor hypothesis by correlating membrane tension with the 2B oligomerization state.

Although this model remains speculative, it generates testable predictions that are amenable to current technology. A key outstanding question concerns residue H53, which has been proposed, purely speculatively, to act as a pH/Ca2+-sensing switch. However, direct structural or mutagenic evidence for this proposed role is not yet available. Resolving the structural basis of 2B gating, including the potential role of H53, represents a critical frontier for understanding how this viroporin couples membrane stress sensing with ion channel activity.

A tentative spatiotemporal framework for 2B function during the viral life cycle is as follows: (i) Early infection (0–3 h post-infection): 2B is translated as part of the P2 polyprotein and inserted into the ER membrane, where it induces calcium leakage. (ii) Replication phase (3–6 h post-infection): 2B oligomerizes and participates in the formation of replication organelles, interacting with 3A, 3AB, and Arf1. During this phase, 2B may induce autophagosome formation to provide membrane scaffolds for replication. (iii) Late infection (6–12 h post-infection): 2B redistributes to the outer mitochondrial membrane and other compartments, where it engages Bax, NLRP3, and immune signaling pathways. We emphasize that this timeline is inferential and based on indirect evidence from multiple studies; direct kinetic analyses of 2B localization and function are required.

sections.title: Hypotheses on the molecular mechanism of conformational dynamics

paragraphs.en: The conformational switch model is shown in Figure 1. Based on the above evidence, three testable mechanistic hypotheses are proposed in this study.

sections.title: Helix-helix allostery hypothesis

paragraphs.en: H1 and H2 of 2B engage in dynamic helix-helix interactions within the membrane, and the interhelical angle is modulated by the membrane lipid composition (e.g. cholesterol content) and curvature. A low-cholesterol environment promotes H1-H2 dissociation, exposing the otherwise buried hydrophobic interfaces. Depending on the membrane compartment, these conformational changes may selectively recruit distinct host factors, such as Bax at the outer mitochondrial membrane and NLRP3 at the ER or ER-derived membranes. Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that cholesterol can markedly alter the membrane insertion behavior of the Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) 2B peptide [62], suggesting that lipid composition influences the 2B conformation. Although this study pertains to HAV, enterovirus 2B may possess similar lipid sensitivity.

sections.title: Stem-loop hinge hypothesis

paragraphs.en: We hypothesized that the stem-loop region may act as a pH-sensitive hinge, potentially undergoing cis-trans isomerization. An alternative explanation is that the protonation of nearby residues (e.g. H53) alters the local electrostatics without backbone isomerization. The rapid degradation of EVD68 2B when vesicle acidification is blocked indicates that its transmembrane region contains amino acid residues capable of sensing pH [39]. It is speculated that the protonation of a histidine residue (H53) in the stem loop is critical for pH sensing (putative, moderate strength, based on indirect evidence of pH-dependent degradation of EVD68 without direct mutational validation). The V56A mutation in CVB3 2B abolishes autophagy induction [45], also supporting the stem-loop region as a key hinge for conformational regulation.

sections.title: The C-terminal variable region as a candidate specificity determinant

paragraphs.en: One possibility is that the length and charge of the C-terminal region dictate selective interactions with different host factors. For example, sequence variations in this region may affect the binding efficiency of 2B to nucleocytoplasmic trafficking factors, such as KPNA1 and ILF2, which could contribute to the functional divergence observed among enteroviruses. This remains to be tested by domain-swapping experiments between EVA71 and CVB3 2B (e.g. replacing the C-terminus of CVB3 2B with that of EVA71 and assessing KPNA1 binding and degradation). An independent line of indirect support comes from FMDV 2B, where the C-terminal- region (aa 105–114) mediates RIG-I binding (see Rational design of antivirals based on the membrane stress sensor hypothesis for cross-virus- comparisons); however, whether a similar mechanism operates in enteroviruses is unknown.

These three hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and may operate in concert with each other. Helix-helix allostery and stem-loop hinge models represent two facets of the same conformational switch: lipid-dependent changes in helix packing (helix-helix allostery) may be transmitted through the stem-loop hinge, whose conformation is further modulated by pH. The C-terminal variable region may dictate which host factors are recognized in each conformational state. Determining the relative contributions of lipid composition, pH, and sequence variation to 2B functional outputs will require systematic mutagenesis combined with conformational monitoring in defined membrane environments.

sections.title: Systematic mapping of key residues

paragraphs.en: By synthesizing existing mutational studies, multiple functionally critical residues and their domain locations have been identified (Table 1). Key residues are predominantly located in the stem-loop region (V56, speculative H53) or at the edges of the transmembrane regions (F17L), suggesting that the conformational flexibility of these regions underlies functional divergence. The N-terminus (aa 22–35) determines Bax binding (EVA71), and the transmembrane region (H2) determines oligomerization and autophagy induction (CVB3). This pattern of “regional functional specialization” provides sequence-level support for the conformational dynamics hypothesis. A sequence alignment of 2B proteins from representative enteroviruses is provided in Figure S1, which illustrates the conservation of these key residues and highlights the contrast between the relatively conserved transmembrane regions and the highly variable C-terminal tails.

sections.title: 2B as a hub for inducing calcium signals: primary effect or downstream consequence?

paragraphs.en: Calcium signaling is a central node in the 2B functional network, with virtually all downstream effects (apoptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy, and immune evasion) linked to calcium. However, a fundamental question remains unresolved: Is the calcium elevation induced by 2B a direct function (acting as a calcium channel) or a consequence of membrane damage?

sections.title: Evidence supporting calcium elevation as a primary effect of 2B

paragraphs.en: Multiple studies have shown that calcium elevation is a direct effect of 2B. Expression of EVA71 2B alone induces a significant increase in cytosolic calcium concentration in SH-SY5Y cells, and this effect precedes the appearance of apoptotic markers (6 h vs 24 h) [63]. Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), mediated by the ER calcium sensor STIM1 and the plasma membrane channel Orai1, is activated upon ER calcium depletion [64]. In the context of 2B expression, activation of the SOCE pathway depends on ER calcium depletion [64], which is directly related to the insertion of 2B into the ER membrane. Upon insertion, the passive release of ER luminal calcium triggers STIM1-Orai1-mediated calcium entry.

Furthermore, 2B-induced calcium elevation was closely associated with mitochondrial function. VDAC3 knockdown significantly suppresses 2B-induced mitochondrial ROS production and reduces the viral replication efficiency [37]. Metabolomic analysis further revealed that VDAC3 deficiency leads to compensatory enhancement of the hypotaurine/taurine synthesis pathway in infected cells as an adaptive response to oxidative stress. Moreover, the functional consequences of 2B-mediated calcium elevation extend to mitochondrial metabolism. This finding places 2B, calcium signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, and viral replication in a single causal chain.

Interestingly, although CVB3 2B also reduces ER calcium content, its ultimate effect is the inhibition rather than promotion of apoptosis [65]. This difference may be related to the viral species or infection stage and suggests that the downstream interpretation of calcium signals is cellular context-dependent.

sections.title: Counterarguments challenging the centrality of calcium

paragraphs.en: Enterovirus 2B forms cation-permeable channels in the ER and Golgi membranes, leading to Ca2+ release into the cytosol and depletion of intraluminal stores [66]. Whether this ER Ca2+ depletion directly modulates STIM1–Orai1 coupling – thereby activating or hijacking the SOCE machinery – or instead represents a secondary consequence of global ER stress, remains to be experimentally determined [67] (see also Broad-spectrum suppression of innate immune signaling pathways). The pore formed by 2B permits the passage of low-molecular-weight solutes and is thought to be largely nonselective for ions [66,68]. If this is the case, “calcium signaling” is a byproduct of membrane damage rather than a precisely regulated process. The key to distinguishing between these two possibilities lies in ion selectivity experiments: if 2B forms a nonselective pore, its permeability to Na+, K+, and Ca2+ should not differ significantly; if 2B is a selective calcium channel, it should exhibit preferential Ca2+ permeability. However, the existing literature does not provide data on ion selectivity. This question can be addressed using planar lipid bilayer electrophysiology experiments.

sections.title: Ion selectivity as the Gold standard to distinguish channel activity from membrane damage

paragraphs.en: To definitively resolve the origin of 2B-induced calcium signals, the following two types of experiments are recommended: (1) Planar lipid bilayer reconstitution assay: Reconstitute purified 2B protein into artificial lipid bilayers, measure the reversal potentials, and calculate the PCa/PNa ratio. A PCa/PNa ratio significantly > 1 would demonstrate calcium selectivity, whereas a ratio of ≈1 would support the non-selective pore hypothesis of calcium transport. (2) Whole-cell patch clamp with ion substitution: Records from 2B-expressing cells and use of calcium channel blockers to distinguish the contribution of 2B from that of endogenous calcium channels. The purification and reconstitution of 2B have been reported [49], and patch-clamp techniques have been applied in enterovirus research [69]; therefore, this experimental scheme is technically feasible.

sections.title: Cell death pathway selection is dictated by membrane environment

paragraphs.en: Through its viroporin activity, the 2B protein induces calcium homeostasis imbalance and oxidative stress, pushing cells to the brink of death. However, enterovirus infection-induced cell death is not a single mode of passive disintegration but an actively regulated process that involves multiple mechanisms. Recent studies have revealed that the differential localization of 2B on various subcellular membrane structures dictates the molecular switch that activates apoptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy, and ferroptosis.

sections.title: 2B protein regulates Apoptosis via bax-dependent and -Independent mechanisms

paragraphs.en: EVA71 2B can directly bind to the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and induce its conformational activation [32]. Under physiological conditions, Bax is distributed in the cytosol in an inactive form. Upon 2B expression, Bax is rapidly recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane, exposing its N-terminal active epitope, undergoing oligomerization, and leading to cytochrome c release and caspase-9 cascade activation. This mechanism is Bax-specific; Bax knockdown significantly inhibits 2B-induced apoptosis, whereas Bak knockdown is ineffective [32]. Notably, although EVA71 2A and 3C also possess apoptosis-inducing ability [70], they rely on their protease activity, whereas 2B achieves this through direct PPI.

CVB3 2B exhibits the opposite function; it inhibits caspase activation and apoptosis by reducing the calcium content in the ER and Golgi, thereby protecting infected cells from premature death [65]. This difference may reflect the fine-tuned regulation of host cell death timing by different viruses during their replication cycles; CVB3 needs to delay apoptosis to complete replication, whereas EVA71 may exploit apoptosis to promote viral release at the late stage of its replication cycle.

Bax activation is membrane environment dependent. EVA71 2B is localized to the mitochondria [32], and its interaction with Bax occurs on the outer mitochondrial membrane. Given the marked differences in lipid composition (e.g. cardiolipin content) between the mitochondrial outer membrane and ER membrane, we speculate that 2B may adopt a specific conformation on the mitochondrial membrane that favors exposure of the Bax-binding domain (aa 22–35) (speculative, moderate strength).

The NLRP3 inflammasome serves as a central cytosolic platform that senses diverse danger signals, including lysosomal damage, mitochondrial ROS, and aberrant Ca2+ flux, and transduces them into inflammatory caspase activation and IL-1β/IL-18 maturation [71]. NLRP3 activation proceeds in two steps: a priming signal (typically NF-κB-dependent transcriptional upregulation of pro-IL-1β and NLRP3 itself) and an activation signal that promotes NLRP3 oligomerization and ASC speck formation. Cytosolic Ca2+ elevation has been specifically implicated in the activation step, raising the possibility that 2B-mediated Ca2+ dysregulation contributes to NLRP3-dependent inflammatory signaling during enterovirus infection [72].

sections.title: 2B protein as a broad-spectrum activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome

paragraphs.en: Pyroptosis is executed by the gasdermin protein family, whose N-terminal pore-forming domain is released upon cleavage by inflammatory caspases. In canonical NLRP3-driven pyroptosis, caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD) to release its N-terminal fragment, which inserts into the plasma membrane to form large (10–20 nm) pores that drive rapid cell lysis and IL-1β secretion [73–75]. A non-canonical pathway, in which caspase-4/5 (human) or caspase-11 (mouse) directly sense cytosolic LPS and cleave GSDMD, provides an additional trigger for pyroptosis independent of NLRP3 [76–78]. In contrast to GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis, caspase-3 can cleave gasdermin E (GSDME) to induce secondary pyroptosis in the context of apoptotic signaling, a mechanistic distinction relevant for interpreting 2B-mediated cell death phenotypes.

Echovirus 11 (EchoV11) 2B has been shown to directly bind to NLRP3 and promotes inflammasome assembly [33]. Expression of EchoV11 2B alone in macrophages is sufficient to induce caspase-1 cleavage, GSDMD activation, and IL-1β secretion, and expression of 2B in the mouse liver activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. In the same study, Wang et al. tested the 2B proteins of other enteroviruses [EVA71, CVB3, and Coxsackievirus A16 (CVA16)] and found that the interaction between 2B and NLRP3 is a broadly conserved function of the enterovirus 2B family [33].

Classical activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome typically requires potassium efflux and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS). 2B-induced calcium leakage could indirectly promote potassium efflux by activating calcium-activated potassium channels. However, it remains to be verified whether potassium efflux is an essential step in 2B-mediated NLRP3 activation. If 2B cannot activate NLRP3 under conditions where the potassium concentration is clamped, the critical mediating role of potassium efflux can be established. The link between 2B-induced calcium elevation and NLRP3 activation is further supported by studies on the encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV). EMCV 2B alone is sufficient to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, and this activation depends on intracellular Ca2+ flux rather than mitochondrial ROS or lysosomal cathepsin B [79]. Notably, the 2B proteins of poliovirus and EVA71 also cause NLRP3 redistribution, suggesting that calcium-dependent NLRP3 activation is a conserved function of picornavirus 2B proteins.

sections.title: The dual role of 2B in autophagy: inducing formation while blocking degradation

paragraphs.en: The relationship between 2B and autophagy is one of the most debated topics in enterovirus research. On the one hand, 2B has been shown to independently induce autophagosome formation. Expression of CVB3 2B alone increases LC3-II conversion and the number of autophagic puncta, and this capacity depends on the transmembrane hydrophobic regions; the V56A mutation in H2 completely abolishes this effect [45]. This “incomplete” autophagy induction benefits viral replication by providing autophagic membrane structures as replication scaffolds while preventing excessive degradation of viral components. In contrast, the stability of 2B during EVD68 infection depends on autophagic flux integrity. As noted above, EVD68 2B is rapidly degraded when vesicle acidification is blocked, a phenomenon not observed for CVB3 or PV.

To unify these observations, we propose that the conformation of 2B differs between distinct membrane compartments (autophagosomal and lysosomal membranes). Whether this differential conformation is achieved through the temporal redistribution of the same 2B molecules or through distinct 2B subpopulations sorted into different membrane compartments remains to be determined. Single-molecule tracking and pulse-chase localization assays are required to distinguish between these two possibilities. On the autophagosomal membrane, 2B adopts a conformation that promotes LC3-II recruitment. On the lysosomal membrane, 2B disrupts the proton gradient through its pore activity, blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Validation approaches include isolating autophagosomal and lysosomal membrane fractions, detecting differences in 2B distribution by immunoblotting, and using pH-sensitive fluorescent probes to monitor the effect of 2B on lysosomal acidity.

This model predicts that 2B stability depends on the integrity of autophagic flux. Consistent with this prediction, a functional link between autophagic flux and 2B stability has been established in EVD68 infection: when vesicle acidification is blocked, EVD68 2B undergoes rapid degradation [39]. Consistent with this observation, starvation after infection (SAI), which induces autophagic flux, attenuates EVD68 replication across multiple cell lines and prevents the formation of virus-induced membranes required for picornavirus replication [80]. Collectively, these findings suggest that EVD68 2B requires an acidic microenvironment for its stability and function, and that disruption of this environment, either pharmacologically (via acidification blockers) or physiologically (via SAI), compromises 2B function and viral replication. Thus, the autophagy-modulating function of 2B is another manifestation of its membrane environment-dependent conformational selection.

sections.title: Ferroptosis: a preliminary link to 2B function

paragraphs.en: A recent study from our group provided the first evidence linking 2B to ferroptosis regulation: CVB3 infection downregulates m6A modification of LONP1 mRNA, leading to LONP1 protein accumulation; LONP1 overexpression inhibits viral replication and ferroptosis by restoring GPX4 activity and suppressing ACSL4 [44]. In this process, 2B degrades the m6A methyltransferase WTAP via the proteasome pathway, reducing m6A modification of LONP1 and stabilizing its transcript. We emphasize that these findings are preliminary and have not yet been independently verified. The mechanism by which 2B mediates WTAP degradation remains unknown, as does the functional significance of 2B MAM localization for this pathway. Given these uncertainties, the proposed 2B–WTAP–LONP1–GPX4 cascade should be considered a working model that requires independent validation in future studies. Its connection to the membrane stress sensor framework, specifically whether 2B conformational changes at MAMs directly regulate WTAP interaction, remains speculative and warrants future investigation.

sections.title: A conformational switch model for divergent 2B functions in cell death

paragraphs.en: Although the above four death mechanisms appear independent, within the “membrane stress sensor” framework, they can be unified by the concept that the conformation of 2B in different membrane compartments dictates which death pathway is activated. As illustrated in Figure 2, the conformation of 2B in each compartment dictates its functional output: a closed conformation on the mitochondrial outer membrane may favor Bax-mediated apoptosis; an open conformation on the ER membrane (or ER-derived vesicles) may favor NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis; an autophagy-inducing conformation on the autophagosomal membrane promotes LC3-II recruitment while blocking lysosomal fusion; and a putative conformation at MAMs may initiate the epigenetic regulation of ferroptosis. Thus, 2B does not simply trigger cell death; it choreographs a spatiotemporally orchestrated cell death program, where its itinerary across different membrane compartments – from the ER to mitochondria to autophagosomes – determines the sequential engagement of pyroptosis and apoptosis and ultimately modulates autophagy and ferroptosis.

Based on this framework, we predicted that altering the microenvironmental parameters of a membrane compartment could directionally switch the death pathway output of 2B. For example, pharmacological depletion of mitochondrial cardiolipin should shift 2B from activating apoptosis to pyroptosis. Conversely, increasing ER membrane cholesterol content may expose the NLRP3-binding domain and confer pyroptotic capacity on 2B or reinforce the open conformation that favors pyroptosis. These predictions can be tested using structure-function correlation experiments. The death pathway preferences of 2B from different viruses (e.g. EVA71 favoring apoptosis and EchoV11 favoring pyroptosis) can be explained by differences in key residues that result in distinct conformational equilibria in different membrane environments.

sections.title: Broad-spectrum suppression of innate immune signaling pathways

paragraphs.en: The 2B protein also suppresses immune response. This dual role of “promoting death with one hand and suppressing immunity with the other” makes 2B a central executor of the enterovirus pathogenic strategy.

sections.title: Virus-specific immune evasion pathways

paragraphs.en: The dual role of 2B in innate immune evasion, encompassing both inhibitory and activating pathways, is illustrated in Figure 3.

sections.title: Interference with the Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway

paragraphs.en: KPNA1 degradation. EVA71 2B induces caspase-3-dependent degradation of KPNA1, blocking p-STAT1/2 nuclear translocation, and rendering cells unresponsive to interferon (IFN)-α stimulation [34]. The N-terminal hydrophilic domain (H1) of 2B plays a critical role in this process. In cells infected with an H1 deletion mutant, KPNA1 degradation was abrogated and sensitivity to IFN-α was restored. This mechanism directly links the ion channel activity of 2B to innate immune evasion, as abnormal calcium signaling is an upstream event in caspase-3 activation. This pathway has only been reported in EVA71 infection.

sections.title: Inhibition of ILF2

paragraphs.en: EVA71 2B interacts with ILF2, inducing its translocation from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and inhibiting its protein expression [35]. ILF2 possesses anti-EVA71 activity, and its downregulation significantly enhances viral replication.

sections.title: Antagonism of CD74

paragraphs.en: CD74, an major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II chaperone, binds to the second hydrophobic region of EVD68 2B and inhibit viral replication [36]. As a countermeasure, EVD68 employs its 3C protease to cleave CD74, thereby relieving its antiviral effect. EVD68, a respiratory enterovirus associated with acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in children, exhibits biennial epidemic waves in North America and Europe. Prospective surveillance during the 2022–2023 period confirmed the continued association between EVD68 and AFM in pediatric patients in the United States [81,82]. In parallel, novel EVD68 subclades with distinct receptor-binding characteristics have been detected in European surveillance networks, suggesting ongoing adaptive evolution [83]. Whether the 2B proteins of these emerging subclades exhibit altered membrane-permeabilizing or immune-modulatory properties compared to prototypic EVD68 strains remains an unexplored question with potential relevance to neurovirulence mechanisms.

sections.title: Mitochondrial DNA release and the cGAS-STING pathway

paragraphs.en: In contrast to the above-mentioned inhibitory functions, 2B also exhibits immune activation potential under certain conditions. Infection with various enteroviruses and other Picornaviridae viruses can induce mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release via 2B, which activates the cGAS-STING-mediated type I interferon response [84]. Mechanistically, cGAS detects cytosolic double-stranded DNA and synthesizes the second messenger cGAMP, which activates the ER-resident adaptor STING to induce type I interferon production [85]. Although viral evasion of cGAS-STING signaling is a conserved immune escape strategy across multiple virus families [86], the virus has evolved a specific countermeasure during infection: the 2C protein degrades cGAS through the autophagy pathway. This “activation–suppression” pairing may reflect the fine-tuned regulation of the immune response by the virus. Whether 2B, beyond its mtDNA-releasing activity, directly subverts cGAS-STING signaling, for instance, by interfering with STING trafficking or cGAMP production, remains an open question. The known host interaction partners of enterovirus 2B and their functional impacts are listed in Table 2.

sections.title: Coupling of calcium signaling and immune evasion

paragraphs.en: These immune evasion mechanisms are tightly coupled to the calcium signaling regulatory function of 2B protein. EVA71 2B-induced KPNA1 degradation depends on caspase-3 activation [34], and caspase-3 activation in turn depends on cytochrome c release triggered by mitochondrial calcium overload [63]. These data suggest the following causal chain: 2B insertion into the ER membrane → calcium leakage → mitochondrial calcium overload → cytochrome c release → caspase-9 activation → caspase-3 activation → KPNA1 degradation → blocked STAT1/2 nuclear translocation. A key link in this chain is whether calcium signaling is an essential upstream event for KPNA1 degradation; this remains to be verified by infecting BAPTA-AM-pretreated cells with EVA71 and detecting the KPNA1 protein levels. If calcium chelation blocks KPNA1 degradation, the central role of calcium signaling in this immune evasion pathway can be confirmed.

sections.title: The interplay between pro-inflammatory signaling and immune evasion

paragraphs.en: Table 3 provides a comparative overview of the functional profiles of 2B across representative enteroviruses. 2B exhibits an “activation–suppression” duality: on the one hand, it activates cGAS-STING through mtDNA release; on the other, it suppresses interferon signaling by degrading KPNA1 and other factors. This is not functional chaos but rather a finely tuned regulatory strategy forged through coevolution. (1) Cost and benefit of activation: Moderate mtDNA release can trigger autophagy (providing replication membrane scaffolds), and the activation intensity is strictly restrained by 2C, maintaining it at a “beneficial” level. (2) Breadth and specificity of suppression: Different viruses suppress different targets; EVA71 focuses on KPNA1 and ILF2, reflecting its adaptation to a specific host environment. (3) Spatiotemporal coordination hypothesis: During early infection, 2B is mainly localized to the ER, inducing calcium signaling and KPNA1 degradation to establish an immunosuppressive state. During the mid-to-late stages of infection, a portion of 2B is translocated to the mitochondria, releasing mtDNA and transiently activating cGAS-STING, which is promptly suppressed by 2C. We emphasize that this spatiotemporal coordination hypothesis is based on indirect evidence and has not yet been experimentally validated. Direct visualization of 2B subcellular redistribution during the course of infection, combined with temporally resolved functional assays, is required to test this model.

sections.title: Evolutionary divergence: molecular footprints of sequence variation

paragraphs.en: The functional diversity of the 2B protein is not randomly distributed but represents adaptive features shaped during evolution. Molecular epidemiological and experimental evolution studies have repeatedly indicated that the 2B coding region is a hotspot for recombination and adaptive mutations in enteroviruses. This pattern, high conservation in the transmembrane “sensor” domain coupled with high variability in the “effector” interfaces, is the hallmark of a sensory protein. Evolutionary pressure preserves the core mechanics of the sensor while constantly modifying its interaction partners to adapt to new host environments.

sections.title: Mechanisms underlying the 2B region as a recombination hotspot

paragraphs.en: Recombination between co-circulating EV strains is a major driver of enterovirus evolution, with breakpoints clustering preferentially in the non-structural coding regions 2B–2C and 3D [87,88]. Post-vaccine introduction surveillance in mainland China has demonstrated a pronounced shift in hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) outbreak composition: widespread EVA71 vaccination since 2016 has suppressed EVA71-associated severe disease but concurrently increased the relative contribution of CVA6, CVA10, and non-EVA71 recombinant strains to the outbreak burden [89]. This epidemiological shift underscores the importance of monitoring 2B sequence diversity across emerging non-EVA71 strains, as vaccine-driven selective pressure may inadvertently enrich strains with distinct 2B functional properties.

The 2B coding region has long been recognized as a recombination hotspot for enteroviruses. Early evidence came from a study of EVA71 isolates in Taiwan between 1986 and 2005, where the 2B region of 2004–2005 isolates clustered with genotype B, while all other genomic regions (5′-UTR, VP4-VP2, VP1, and 3D) clustered with genotype C, indicating intratypic recombination within the 2B coding region [90]. Molecular epidemiological studies have shown that the 2B coding region is a hotspot for interspecies/intertype recombination in enteroviruses. The 2B region of an E30 recombinant strain originated from recombination between E30 and other EV-B members [91]; the 2B gene of an E18 recombinant strain recombined with E30 [92]; Coxsackievirus A6 recombined with EVA114 in the 2B region [93]; the recombination breakpoint of a novel EVA71 subgenotype C6 is located at the 2A/2B junction [94,95]; characteristic mutations C3277A and A4020G of a 2014 US EVD68 outbreak strain are also located in the 2B flanking region [96]; and during consecutive alternating antiviral treatment, specific mutations emerged in the 2B region of Coxsackievirus B1 [97]. Moreover, PV progressively became independent of the PI4KB/OSBP pathway during evolution through the 2B-F17L and 2B-Q20H mutations [98], further demonstrating the key role of 2B in viral adaptation. Most recently, genomic surveillance in Maryland in 2025 identified a novel EVD68 A2/B3 recombinant with the recombination breakpoint precisely mapped to the 2A/2B junction [99]. This finding further underscores the 2B-encoding region as a frequent recombination hotspot.

This recombination hotspot status is not coincidental but reflects the central role of the 2B protein in evolution: 2B is the center of tension between evolutionary plasticity and functional conservation. In terms of conservation, the basic functions of 2B, transmembrane topology, membrane insertion ability, and oligomerization, are highly conserved and mediated by relatively conserved transmembrane regions and critical stem-loop residues (e.g. V56). In terms of plasticity, the C-terminal variable region, stem-loop edge residues, and interaction interfaces of 2B show high variability, allowing the virus to acquire new functions (e.g. immune evasion and death pathway selection) and adapt to new ecological niches.

sections.title: Trans-complementation and evolutionary plasticity

paragraphs.en: The E40K mutation in CVB3 2B produces a quasi-infectious phenotype that can be rescued by trans-complementation with the wild-type virus [40]. This is the first report that a genetic defect in an enterovirus 2B protein can be trans-complemented, suggesting that 2B function can be “rescued” at the viral population level. This finding has important evolutionary implications: defective mutants can be “helped” by wild-type 2B through co-infection, thereby maintaining their presence in the population, increasing genetic diversity, and providing a “reservoir” for adaptation to new environments. This implies that drugs targeting 2B may need to achieve a high level of population inhibition; otherwise, a small number of wild-type viruses may “rescue” drug-resistant mutants through trans-complementation. In contrast, an insertion mutant of PV 2B cannot be trans-complemented [100], suggesting that certain functions of 2B may act in cis, further adding to the complexity of 2B functional regulation.

sections.title: The tension between conservancy and druggability

paragraphs.en: The 2B sequence is generally conserved across the Enterovirus genus (especially the transmembrane regions); however, functionally critical residues are highly variable. From a drug development perspective, this feature constitutes a tension: targeting conserved domains (e.g. the stem-loop hinge region) may achieve broad-spectrum activity, but it must be verified whether this region plays a similar conformational regulatory role across diverse viruses; targeting variable regions (e.g. the C-terminus) can achieve virus specificity but requires the design of different inhibitors for different viruses. This tension is both a challenge and an opportunity, suggesting that a combined strategy targeting multiple domains may be optimal.

sections.title: Rational design of antivirals based on the membrane stress sensor hypothesis

paragraphs.en: The pleiotropic roles of 2B in viral replication and pathogenesis make it a compelling target for anti-enterovirus drug development. Existing strategies have largely focused on blocking pore-forming activity and silencing expression. However, none of these studies have targeted the core mechanism proposed here, that is, the ability of 2B to sense the membrane microenvironment and transduce signals through conformational changes. Based on the theoretical framework of the “membrane stress sensor” proposed above, three categories of targeting strategies are presented below. These strategies are schematically summarized in Figure 4.

The druggability of enterovirus 2B has been substantiated by a growing body of experimental evidence, which can be broadly categorized into channel blockers, oligomerization disruptors, and gene silencing approaches. A comprehensive review by Peng et al. cataloged various small-molecule inhibitors targeting viral ion channels, highlighting the potential of viroporins as antiviral targets. Among these, the anion channel inhibitor DIDS (4,4”-diisothiocyano-2,2”−stilbenedisulfonic acid) has been shown to block the chloride-dependent current mediated by the EV71 2B protein in Xenopus oocytes and, more importantly, to significantly reduce viral titers and cytopathic effects in cell culture [69,101]. Furthermore, a Tat-2B (37–50) peptide, which competitively binds to the H2 transmembrane region, has been shown to inhibit CVB3 infection by interfering with 2B oligomerization [43]. RNA interference approaches have also proven effective, as synthetic siRNAs targeting the 2B coding region of EVA71 markedly reduced viral replication in vitro [42]. Collectively, these studies provide compelling proof-of-concept validation that 2B is a druggable target and that interfering with its channel function, oligomerization, or expression can effectively suppress enterovirus replication.

Strategy 1: Conformational locking. Small molecules that specifically lock 2B into one conformational state (closed or open) block its response to changes in the membrane microenvironment. Ideal targets include the conserved stem-loop hinge region (containing V56 and the putative pH-sensing residue H53) and the H1-H2 interaction interface of the proteins. Strategies targeting these conserved domains are expected to achieve broad-spectrum anti-enteroviral activity. As they directly intervene in conformational dynamics, the virus must acquire multiple mutations to escape, resulting in a high resistance barrier. A previously reported Tat-2B (37–50) derivative peptide may interfere with oligomerization by competitively binding to the H2 region [43], and its mode of action can be considered a type of conformational perturbant.

Strategy 2: Membrane environment disruptors. Pharmacological agents that alter membrane microenvironmental parameters, thereby indirectly influencing the membrane localization, conformational selection, and functional execution of 2B. Cholesterol chelators (e.g. methyl-β-cyclodextrin) disrupt lipid raft structures and interfere with the enrichment of 2B in specific membrane microdomains. pH modulators (e.g. bafilomycin A1) can alter the acidification state of endosomes or lysosomes, blocking the pH-dependent activation of 2B. Cardiolipin synthesis inhibitors may interfere with the 2B function of the mitochondrial membrane. The advantage lies in the indirect mode of action, which makes it difficult for the virus to develop resistance merely through mutations in 2B. However, the challenge is the relatively high risk of off-target effects of these therapies. No direct studies have been conducted yet, but based on our hypothesis, these tool drugs may be effective.

Strategy 3: Interaction interface blockers. Direct disruption of the binding of 2B to critical host factors is also possible. The priority targets include the Bax-binding domain of EVA71 (aa 22–35), whose blockade can inhibit apoptosis; the putative NLRP3-binding domain, whose blockade can inhibit pyroptosis; and regions involved in KPNA1 degradation, whose intervention can restore interferon signaling. The advantage of this method is its high specificity; however, the challenge is the difficulty in screening PPI inhibitors.

Based on the evidence strength and sequence conservation analysis, the following two classes of targets are recommended for priority development: (1) Stem-loop hinge region: This region is relatively conserved among enteroviruses (V56 is ubiquitous) and is critical for conformational change. Structure-based virtual screening can be used to identify small molecules that bind to the 2B region. (2) Bax/NLRP3 interaction interfaces: The Bax-binding domain has been precisely mapped in EVA71, and NLRP3 activation is conserved across a diverse range of enteroviruses. Phage display can be used to screen for blocking peptides. Considering the potential resistance issues arising from trans-complementation, a combination targeting strategy is expected to inhibit viral replication more effectively and increase the resistance barrier.

sections.title: Cross-virus comparisons: insights from other Picornaviridae members

paragraphs.en: Although this review focuses on enteroviruses, studies on the 2B proteins of other picornaviruses provide valuable parallel evidence for understanding enterovirus 2B function. FMDV 2B possesses two independent pore domains [102], and its C-terminal region (aa105–114) mediates RIG-I degradation [103], suggesting that pore activity and immune evasion functions can coexist within the same molecule but may be executed by different domains. Senecavirus A (SVA) 2B maintains stability through interactions with HSP70/HSP90 [104] and degrades Stimulator of Interferon Genes (STING) and Mitochondrial Antiviral Signaling protein (MAVS) [105,106], indicating that molecular chaperones may participate in the conformational regulation of 2B. EMCV produces a 2B variant via frameshifting [107], whose function differs from that of canonical 2B, suggesting a more complex coding capacity at the 2B locus. The crystal structure of the soluble domain of HAV 2B revealed a curved five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet followed by a C-terminal helical bundle, providing the first structural model for 2B-induced membrane remodeling [108]. HAV 2B is significantly larger (~250 aa), and its C-terminus possesses lipid-specific pore activity that is regulated by cholesterol [62,109], indicating that membrane lipid sensing may be a conserved property of picornavirus 2B proteins, although HAV 2B is functionally deficient in calcium signaling and protein transport inhibition. These cross-virus comparisons suggest that the core elements of the “membrane stress sensor” framework (membrane lipid sensing and conformational dynamics) may be conserved to varying degrees within Picornaviridae, but specific functional execution (especially immune evasion) is highly species-specific (Table S1). Therefore, this framework provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding enterovirus 2B, but its applicability to other genera is only of reference value. Interestingly, 2B can also serve as a T-cell epitope; T-cell lines from healthy donors recognize CVB4 2B [110], suggesting that 2B may contribute to adaptive immune recognition despite its role in immune evasion.

sections.title: Conclusions and outlook

paragraphs.en: This study proposes an integrative framework in which the enterovirus 2B protein acts as a “membrane stress sensor,” thereby overcoming the limitations of the traditional viroporin model. Through conformational dynamics, the transmembrane helices of 2B sense changes in the membrane microenvironment (lipid composition, pH, and curvature) and coordinate calcium signaling, cell death pathway selection, and immune evasion outputs in a spatiotemporally specific manner. This framework provides a unified explanation for the direct interactions of 2B with host factors such as Bax, NLRP3, and KPNA1, the functional divergence among different viruses, and the evolutionary footprint of the 2B region as a recombination hotspot.

sections.title: Key uncertainties

paragraphs.en: (1) Does 2B exhibit calcium ion selectivity, or does it form a nonselective pore? However, direct evidence from planar lipid bilayer electrophysiology experiments is required. (2) Is the pH dependence of EVD68 2B mediated by a specific histidine residue (e.g. H53)? Site-directed mutagenesis and functional assays under controlled pH conditions are required. (3) The specific molecular mechanism by which 2B blocks autophagosome-lysosome fusion remains to be elucidated. (4) Does 2B degrade WTAP via the calcium–calpain pathway or through another mechanism? Direct verification is required. (5) Direct conformational evidence of 2B in different membrane environments is still lacking, and NMR or cryo-EM studies are required. (6) The membrane stress sensor framework remains a hypothesis. Direct experimental evidence for lipid- or pH-dependent conformational switching of 2B is required to validate or refute this model.

A comparative perspective on viroporin biology illuminates both the conserved principles and unique features of 2B. The Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) p7 and influenza M2 viroporins have yielded tractable targets for antiviral drug development: amantadine and rimantadine block M2-mediated proton conductance, while a broad array of alkylated imino-sugar derivatives inhibits p7 channel activity. These precedents validate the viroporin channel as an antiviral druggable target and encourage analogous pharmacological exploration of enterovirus 2B. The membrane stress sensor framework proposed here extends beyond 2B, and similar conformational coupling between the membrane physical properties and channel gating may represent a broader strategy exploited by diverse viroporins. Future structure-guided drug design targeting the 2B gating interface or its lipid-binding determinants may benefit from the lessons learned from the M2 and p7 systems.

sections.title: Future directions

paragraphs.en: To validate the membrane stress sensor hypothesis, the following directions are proposed as future priorities: (1) Structural elucidation: Determine the high-resolution structures of 2B in different membrane environments using cryo-EM or solid-state NMR, and directly test the predicted “open” and “closed” states. (2) Verification of conformational dynamics: FRET-based live-cell conformational reporter systems will be developed to monitor real-time conformational changes in 2B during infection. (3) Targeted intervention: Development of small-molecule inhibitors based on the stem-loop hinge region and interaction interfaces, followed by validation of their antiviral efficacy. (4) Pathogenic mechanisms: Elucidate how differences in the membrane environment of 2B in different tissues/cell types determine viral pathogenicity. (5) Cross-virus comparisons: Systematically compare the conformational dynamics and membrane environment responsiveness of 2B proteins from different picornavirus genera to test whether the “membrane stress sensor” concept has a broader applicability. This framework offers a mechanistic basis for anti-enterovirus drug design and may inform studies on other viroporins with similarly broad functional repertoires.

figures.caption: Topological model and conformational switch hypothesis of enterovirus 2B protein. (A) type IIB topology of EVA71 2B in the ER membrane. Two helical hairpins (H1 and H2) are connected by a luminal stem-loop, and both termini face the cytosol. Solid lines indicate experimentally validated features: V56 (autophagy induction) and N-terminal Bax-binding domain (aa 22–35). Dashed outlines indicate speculative elements: H53 (putative pH sensor) and C-terminal variable region. (B) membrane microenvironment-driven conformational changes. in the mitochondrial outer membrane (cardiolipin-enriched, high curvature), a “closed” conformation exposes the Bax-binding interface, promoting apoptosis. in the ER membrane or ER-derived vesicles (neutral pH, low cholesterol, low curvature), an “open” conformation exposes a putative NLRP3-binding surface, promoting pyroptosis or immune evasion. The switch is triggered by the lipid composition, pH, and curvature (bidirectional arrow). Dashed outlines indicate speculative elements that are components of the membrane stress sensor hypothesis and await direct experimental confirmation. See the evidence grading section in the main text for a comprehensive explanation of the evidence categories. Note that panel (A) depicts the basal topology of 2B in the ER membrane; it is not intended to represent a specific conformational state. The open/closed conformational switch depicted in (B) is a theoretical model based on indirect evidence, and direct structural validation is required.

figures.caption: Compartment-specific conformations of 2B direct four-cell death pathways. The 2B protein (center) acts as a membrane-embedded sensor, with its functional output dictated by its resident compartment. upper left: at the outer mitochondrial membrane, 2B directly activates Bax, leading to cytochrome c release and caspase-9/3 activation (apoptosis) [32]. upper right: at plasma or ER-derived membranes, the 2B-NLRP3 interaction promotes inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, and IL-1β release (pyroptosis) [33]; K+ efflux is a potential intermediate (dashed arrow). lower left: in a V56-dependent manner [45], CVB3 2B induces LC3-II conversion and autophagosome formation while blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion, a pH-dependent step in EVD68 presumed to involve disruption of the lysosomal proton gradient [39]. lower right: CVB3 2B promotes the proteasomal degradation of the m6A methyltransferase WTAP, reducing LONP1 mRNA m6A modification and leading to LONP1 accumulation, GPX4 restoration, and suppression of ferroptosis [44]. The mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs) localization of 2B and the upstream trigger for WTAP degradation (Ca2+ vs direct interaction) remain speculative (dashed lines). Solid arrows, experimentally supported steps; dashed arrows, proposed mechanisms. This figure provides an overview of the four cell death pathways regulated by 2B; each pathway is detailed in Future directions–5.4.
